angles.drive: You prove things rather than announce them. Talk never felt like enough evidence to you, so you keep quiet and make the thing that settles it. You pay for being right this way in years instead of minutes, and you rarely regret the trade.

You say the plain thing and let it land. Honesty is the one performance you refuse to fake, so you say it bluntly instead of gently. You lose a little warmth each time, and you count that a fair price for the truth.

Breaking a rule interests you less than replacing it. Because you would rather make the better way than complain about the old, you rewrite the rule in the doing. You go the slow way instead of the loud one, and what you make holds.

You push back on a thing before you have looked at it. Disagreeing fits you better than nodding does, so you push first and judge later. You know that some of what you pushed against was on your side.

You say the extra sentence, the one the moment did not need. Holding a thought in feels more dishonest than letting it out, so the clever version wins over the quiet one. You know saying less would have said the same thing.

You overdo it on purpose, since enough never felt like a safe place to stop. Making it bigger is more your style than making it done, so every small job grows a second floor. Remember that the second floor comes out of your own supply.

Breaking new ground is how your expression works: the flat, settled, everyone-agrees surface is exactly where you start digging. Your best ideas arrive as polite earthquakes, reorganizing a topic people thought was finished. The field is never as settled as it looks, and you prove it.

Dry is your native register. The joke arrives flat, two beats late, and lands harder for it, usually while everyone else is still being earnest. Humor is how your truth gets past security. People laugh first and only later notice what you actually said.

Doing it the standard way physically bothers you, the way a crooked picture frame bothers other people. Your methods look wrong until the results arrive. The spreadsheet is shaped strangely, the pitch skips the template, and both work for reasons the template never considered.

Disagreeing arrives before your reasons do, and sometimes instead of them. Whatever the group settles on, something in you stands up to unsettle it. Being the counterweight was useful so often that it became a reflex, and now it fires even when the scale was balanced.

Contempt leaks out of you through the smallest muscles, and everyone catches it. The sigh, the half-second stare at the ceiling, the pen set down slowly. You never said the meeting was stupid. Your face published a full review before your mouth said anything.

Long stillness, then the crack: your frustration stores itself quietly and spends itself all at once. Months of fine, fine, fine, and then one Tuesday the ground moves and everyone nearby learns what was actually underneath. The eruption feels sudden to them. It was years old to you.
